    34→def to_wkt(
    35→    geometry,
    36→    rounding_precision=6,
    37→    trim=True,
    38→    output_dimension=None,
    39→    old_3d=False,
    40→    **kwargs,
    41→):
    42→    """Convert to the Well-Known Text (WKT) representation of a Geometry.
    43→
    44→    The Well-known Text format is defined in the `OGC Simple Features
    45→    Specification for SQL <https://www.opengeospatial.org/standards/sfs>`__.
    46→
    47→    The following limitations apply to WKT serialization:
    48→
    49→    - only simple empty geometries can be 3D, empty collections are always 2D
    50→
    51→    Parameters
    52→    ----------
    53→    geometry : Geometry or array_like
    54→        Geometry or geometries to convert to WKT.
    55→    rounding_precision : int, default 6
    56→        The rounding precision when writing the WKT string. Set to a value of
    57→        -1 to indicate the full precision.
    58→    trim : bool, default True
    59→        If True, trim unnecessary decimals (trailing zeros).
    60→    output_dimension : int, default None
    61→        The output dimension for the WKT string. Supported values are 2, 3 and
    62→        4 for GEOS 3.12+. Default None will automatically choose 3 or 4,
    63→        depending on the version of GEOS.
    64→        Specifying 3 means that up to 3 dimensions will be written but 2D
    65→        geometries will still be represented as 2D in the WKT string.
    66→    old_3d : bool, default False
    67→        Enable old style 3D/4D WKT generation. By default, new style 3D/4D WKT
    68→        (ie. "POINT Z (10 20 30)") is returned, but with ``old_3d=True``
    69→        the WKT will be formatted in the style "POINT (10 20 30)".
    70→    **kwargs
    71→        See :ref:`NumPy ufunc docs <ufuncs.kwargs>` for other keyword arguments.
    72→
    73→    Examples
    74→    --------
    75→    >>> from shapely import Point
    76→    >>> to_wkt(Point(0, 0))
    77→    'POINT (0 0)'
    78→    >>> to_wkt(Point(0, 0), rounding_precision=3, trim=False)
    79→    'POINT (0.000 0.000)'
    80→    >>> to_wkt(Point(0, 0), rounding_precision=-1, trim=False)
    81→    'POINT (0.0000000000000000 0.0000000000000000)'
    82→    >>> to_wkt(Point(1, 2, 3), trim=True)
    83→    'POINT Z (1 2 3)'
    84→    >>> to_wkt(Point(1, 2, 3), trim=True, output_dimension=2)
    85→    'POINT (1 2)'
    86→    >>> to_wkt(Point(1, 2, 3), trim=True, old_3d=True)
    87→    'POINT (1 2 3)'
    88→
    89→    Notes
    90→    -----
    91→    The defaults differ from the default of the GEOS library. To mimic this,
    92→    use::
    93→
    94→        to_wkt(geometry, rounding_precision=-1, trim=False, output_dimension=2)
    95→
    96→    """
    97→    if not np.isscalar(rounding_precision):
    98→        raise TypeError("rounding_precision only accepts scalar values")
    99→    if not np.isscalar(trim):
   100→        raise TypeError("trim only accepts scalar values")
   101→    if output_dimension is None:

   110→        np.intc(rounding_precision),

   118→def to_wkb(
   119→    geometry,
   120→    hex=False,
   121→    output_dimension=None,
   122→    byte_order=-1,
   123→    include_srid=False,
   124→    flavor="extended",
   125→    **kwargs,
   126→):
   127→    r"""Convert to the Well-Known Binary (WKB) representation of a Geometry.
   128→
   129→    The Well-Known Binary format is defined in the `OGC Simple Features
   130→    Specification for SQL <https://www.opengeospatial.org/standards/sfs>`__.
   131→
   132→    The following limitations apply to WKB serialization:
   133→
   134→    - linearrings will be converted to linestrings
   135→    - a point with only NaN coordinates is converted to an empty point
   136→
   137→    Parameters
   138→    ----------
   139→    geometry : Geometry or array_like
   140→        Geometry or geometries to convert to WKB.
   141→    hex : bool, default False
   142→        If true, export the WKB as a hexadecimal string. The default is to
   143→        return a binary bytes object.
   144→    output_dimension : int, default None
   145→        The output dimension for the WKB. Supported values are 2, 3 and 4 for
   146→        GEOS 3.12+. Default None will automatically choose 3 or 4, depending on
   147→        the version of GEOS.
   148→        Specifying 3 means that up to 3 dimensions will be written but 2D
   149→        geometries will still be represented as 2D in the WKB representation.
   150→    byte_order : int, default -1
   151→        Defaults to native machine byte order (-1). Use 0 to force big endian
   152→        and 1 for little endian.
   153→    include_srid : bool, default False
   154→        If True, the SRID is be included in WKB (this is an extension
   155→        to the OGC WKB specification). Not allowed when flavor is "iso".
   156→    flavor : {"iso", "extended"}, default "extended"
   157→        Which flavor of WKB will be returned. The flavor determines how
   158→        extra dimensionality is encoded with the type number, and whether
   159→        SRID can be included in the WKB. ISO flavor is "more standard" for
   160→        3D output, and does not support SRID embedding.
   161→        Both flavors are equivalent when ``output_dimension=2`` (or with 2D
   162→        geometries) and ``include_srid=False``.
   163→        The `from_wkb` function can read both flavors.
   164→    **kwargs
   165→        See :ref:`NumPy ufunc docs <ufuncs.kwargs>` for other keyword arguments.
   166→
   167→    Examples
   168→    --------
   169→    >>> from shapely import Point
   170→    >>> point = Point(1, 1)
   171→    >>> to_wkb(point, byte_order=1)
   172→    b'\x01\x01\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\xf0?\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\xf0?'
   173→    >>> to_wkb(point, hex=True, byte_order=1)
   174→    '0101000000000000000000F03F000000000000F03F'
   175→
   176→    """
   177→    if not np.isscalar(hex):
   178→        raise TypeError("hex only accepts scalar values")
   179→    if output_dimension is None:
   180→        output_dimension = 3 if geos_version < (3, 12, 0) else 4
   181→    elif not np.isscalar(output_dimension):
   182→        raise TypeError("output_dimension only accepts scalar values")
   183→    if not np.isscalar(byte_order):
   184→        raise TypeError("byte_order only accepts scalar values")
   185→    if not np.isscalar(include_srid):
   186→        raise TypeError("include_srid only accepts scalar values")
   187→    if not np.isscalar(flavor):
   188→        raise TypeError("flavor only accepts scalar values")
   189→    if lib.geos_version < (3, 10, 0) and flavor == "iso":
   190→        raise UnsupportedGEOSVersionError(
   191→            'The "iso" option requires at least GEOS 3.10.0'
   192→        )
   193→    if flavor == "iso" and include_srid:
   194→        raise ValueError('flavor="iso" and include_srid=True cannot be used together')
   195→    flavor = WKBFlavorOptions.get_value(flavor)
   196→
   197→    return lib.to_wkb(
   198→        geometry,
   199→        np.bool_(hex),
   200→        np.intc(output_dimension),
   201→        np.intc(byte_order),
   202→        np.bool_(include_srid),
   203→        np.intc(flavor),
   204→        **kwargs,
   205→    )

   212→    The GeoJSON format is defined in the `RFC 7946 <https://geojson.org/>`__.

   220→    Parameters
   221→    ----------
   222→    geometry : str, bytes or array_like

   224→    indent : int, optional
   225→        If indent is a non-negative integer, then GeoJSON will be formatted.
   226→        An indent level of 0 will only insert newlines. None (the default)

   240→      "coordinates": [

   242→          1.0

   249→    # - support 3D: https://trac.osgeo.org/geos/ticket/1141

   262→
   263→    The Well-known Text format is defined in the `OGC Simple Features
   264→    Specification for SQL <https://www.opengeospatial.org/standards/sfs>`__.

   266→    Parameters
   267→    ----------
   268→    geometry : str or array_like
   269→        The WKT string(s) to convert.
   270→    on_invalid : {"raise", "warn", "ignore"}, default "raise"

   272→        - warn: a warning will be raised and invalid WKT geometries will be

   274→        - ignore: invalid WKT geometries will be returned as ``None`` without a warning.

   277→
   278→    Examples
   279→    --------
   280→    >>> from_wkt('POINT (0 0)')
   281→    <POINT (0 0)>
   282→
   283→    """
   284→    if not np.isscalar(on_invalid):
   285→        raise TypeError("on_invalid only accepts scalar values")

   287→    invalid_handler = np.uint8(DecodingErrorOptions.get_value(on_invalid))

   292→def from_wkb(geometry, on_invalid="raise", **kwargs):
   293→    r"""Create geometries from the Well-Known Binary (WKB) representation.
   294→
   295→    The Well-Known Binary format is defined in the `OGC Simple Features
   296→    Specification for SQL <https://www.opengeospatial.org/standards/sfs>`__.
   297→
   298→    Parameters
   299→    ----------
   300→    geometry : str or array_like
   301→        The WKB byte object(s) to convert.
   302→    on_invalid : {"raise", "warn", "ignore"}, default "raise"
   303→        - raise: an exception will be raised if a WKB input geometry is invalid.
   304→        - warn: a warning will be raised and invalid WKB geometries will be
   305→          returned as ``None``.
   306→        - ignore: invalid WKB geometries will be returned as ``None`` without a warning.
   307→    **kwargs
   308→        See :ref:`NumPy ufunc docs <ufuncs.kwargs>` for other keyword arguments.
   309→
   310→    Examples
   311→    --------
   312→    >>> from_wkb(b'\x01\x01\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\xf0?\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\xf0?')
   313→    <POINT (1 1)>
   314→
   315→    """  # noqa: E501
   316→    if not np.isscalar(on_invalid):
   317→        raise TypeError("on_invalid only accepts scalar values")

   322→    # fixed-length string dtype (which removes trailing null bytes upon access

    with pytest.raises(
        shapely.GEOSException,

def test_wkt_loads_fix_structure_autocloses_ring():
    # When fix_structure=True, the reader should automatically close the ring
    invalid_poly_wkt = "POLYGON ((0 0, 1 0, 1 1, 0 1))"
    # Expected polygon (Shapely will standardize orientation and close ring)
    expected = Polygon([(0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1)])

    poly = wkt.loads(invalid_poly_wkt, fix_structure=True)

    assert_geometries_equal(poly, expected)


def test_wkt_loads_fix_structure_nested_geometrycollection():
    # Ensure fix_structure applies even within nested collections
    invalid_nested_wkt = (
        "GEOMETRYCOLLECTION (POINT (0 0), GEOMETRYCOLLECTION (POLYGON ((0 0, 1 0, 1 1, 0 1))))"
    )

    inner_collection = parts_lvl1[1]

    expected_nested_poly = Polygon([(0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1)])
    assert_geometries_equal(nested_poly, expected_nested_poly)

def _close_ring_if_needed(ring_str):
    # ring_str like "0 0, 1 0, 1 1, 0 1" possibly with extra spaces
    points = [p.strip() for p in ring_str.strip().split(",") if p.strip()]
    if len(points) < 2:
        return ring_str  # nothing to do

    def _parse_point(pt):
        # supports XY, XYZ, XYM, XYZM
        parts = [x for x in pt.strip().split() if x]
        try:
            return tuple(float(x) for x in parts)
        except ValueError:
            # if parsing fails, keep original (don't change structure)
            return None

    first = _parse_point(points[0])
    last = _parse_point(points[-1])
    if first is None or last is None:
        return ring_str

    if first == last:
        return ring_str  # already closed

    # Append the first point to close the ring
    return ", ".join(points + [points[0]])


def _fix_wkt_structure(data):
    # Only attempt to fix POLYGON rings; leave other types unchanged
    s = data
    out = []
    i = 0
    pattern = re.compile(r"POLYGON", re.IGNORECASE)
    while True:
        m = pattern.search(s, i)
        if not m:
            out.append(s[i:])
            break
        # append text before POLYGON
        out.append(s[i:m.start()])
        out.append(s[m.start():m.end()])  # 'POLYGON'
        # move index after 'POLYGON'
        j = m.end()
        # skip whitespace
        while j < len(s) and s[j].isspace():
            out.append(s[j])
            j += 1
        if j >= len(s) or s[j] != "(":
            # not a valid POLYGON structure, continue
            i = j
            continue
        # append opening parenthesis and capture the content within matching paren
        out.append("(")
        j += 1
        # capture content until matching closing ')'
        depth = 1
        content_start = j
        while j < len(s) and depth > 0:
            if s[j] == "(":
                depth += 1
            elif s[j] == ")":
                depth -= 1
            j += 1
        content = s[content_start : j - 1] if depth == 0 else s[content_start:]
        # Now content should be like '((ring1), (ring2), ...)' without the outer closing
        # We need to iterate rings between parentheses at depth 1 inside content
        rings = []
        k = 0
        while k < len(content):
            # skip whitespace and commas
            while k < len(content) and content[k] in " \t\n,":
                rings.append(content[k]) if False else None  # no-op to keep style
                k += 1
            if k < len(content) and content[k] == "(":
                # find ring content
                k += 1
                ring_start = k
                nest = 1
                while k < len(content) and nest > 0:
                    if content[k] == "(":
                        nest += 1
                    elif content[k] == ")":
                        nest -= 1
                    k += 1
                ring_content = content[ring_start : k - 1]
                fixed_ring = _close_ring_if_needed(ring_content)
                rings.append("(")
                rings.append(fixed_ring)
                rings.append(")")
            else:
                # copy other characters (commas/spaces)
                if k < len(content):
                    rings.append(content[k])
                    k += 1
        fixed_content = "".join(rings)
        out.append(fixed_content)
        out.append(")")
        i = j
    return "".join(out)

    """Load a geometry from a WKT string.

   118→@multithreading_enabled
   119→def buffer(
   120→    geometry,
   121→    distance,
   122→    quad_segs=8,
   123→    cap_style="round",
   124→    join_style="round",
   125→    mitre_limit=5.0,
   126→    single_sided=False,
   127→    **kwargs,
   128→):
   129→    """Compute the buffer of a geometry for positive and negative buffer distance.
   130→
   131→    The buffer of a geometry is defined as the Minkowski sum (or difference,
   132→    for negative distance) of the geometry with a circle with radius equal
   133→    to the absolute value of the buffer distance.
   134→
   135→    The buffer operation always returns a polygonal result. The negative
   136→    or zero-distance buffer of lines and points is always empty.
   137→
   138→    Parameters
   139→    ----------
   140→    geometry : Geometry or array_like
   141→        Geometry or geometries for which to compute the buffer.
   142→    distance : float or array_like
   143→        Specifies the circle radius in the Minkowski sum (or difference).
   144→    quad_segs : int, default 8
   145→        Specifies the number of linear segments in a quarter circle in the
   146→        approximation of circular arcs.
   147→    cap_style : shapely.BufferCapStyle or {'round', 'square', 'flat'}, default 'round'
   148→        Specifies the shape of buffered line endings. BufferCapStyle.round ('round')
   149→        results in circular line endings (see ``quad_segs``). Both BufferCapStyle.square
   150→        ('square') and BufferCapStyle.flat ('flat') result in rectangular line endings,
   151→        only BufferCapStyle.flat ('flat') will end at the original vertex,
   152→        while BufferCapStyle.square ('square') involves adding the buffer width.
   153→    join_style : shapely.BufferJoinStyle or {'round', 'mitre', 'bevel'}, default 'round'
   154→        Specifies the shape of buffered line midpoints. BufferJoinStyle.round ('round')
   155→        results in rounded shapes. BufferJoinStyle.bevel ('bevel') results in a beveled
   156→        edge that touches the original vertex. BufferJoinStyle.mitre ('mitre') results
   157→        in a single vertex that is beveled depending on the ``mitre_limit`` parameter.
   158→    mitre_limit : float, default 5.0
   159→        Crops of 'mitre'-style joins if the point is displaced from the
   160→        buffered vertex by more than this limit.
   161→    single_sided : bool, default False
   162→        Only buffer at one side of the geometry.
   163→    **kwargs
   164→        See :ref:`NumPy ufunc docs <ufuncs.kwargs>` for other keyword arguments.
   165→
   166→    Examples
   167→    --------
   168→    >>> from shapely import LineString, Point, Polygon, BufferCapStyle, BufferJoinStyle
   169→    >>> buffer(Point(10, 10), 2, quad_segs=1)
   170→    <POLYGON ((12 10, 10 8, 8 10, 10 12, 12 10))>
   171→    >>> buffer(Point(10, 10), 2, quad_segs=2)
   172→    <POLYGON ((12 10, 11.414 8.586, 10 8, 8.586 8.586, 8 10, 8.5...>
   173→    >>> buffer(Point(10, 10), -2, quad_segs=1)
   174→    <POLYGON EMPTY>
   175→    >>> line = LineString([(10, 10), (20, 10)])
   176→    >>> buffer(line, 2, cap_style="square")
   177→    <POLYGON ((20 12, 22 12, 22 8, 10 8, 8 8, 8 12, 20 12))>
   178→    >>> buffer(line, 2, cap_style="flat")
   179→    <POLYGON ((20 12, 20 8, 10 8, 10 12, 20 12))>
   180→    >>> buffer(line, 2, single_sided=True, cap_style="flat")
   181→    <POLYGON ((20 10, 10 10, 10 12, 20 12, 20 10))>
   182→    >>> line2 = LineString([(10, 10), (20, 10), (20, 20)])
   183→    >>> buffer(line2, 2, cap_style="flat", join_style="bevel")
   184→    <POLYGON ((18 12, 18 20, 22 20, 22 10, 20 8, 10 8, 10 12, 18 12))>
   185→    >>> buffer(line2, 2, cap_style="flat", join_style="mitre")
   186→    <POLYGON ((18 12, 18 20, 22 20, 22 8, 10 8, 10 12, 18 12))>
   187→    >>> buffer(line2, 2, cap_style="flat", join_style="mitre", mitre_limit=1)
   188→    <POLYGON ((18 12, 18 20, 22 20, 22 9.172, 20.828 8, 10 8, 10 12, 18 12))>
   189→    >>> square = Polygon([(0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 10), (0, 10), (0, 0)])
   190→    >>> buffer(square, 2, join_style="mitre")
   191→    <POLYGON ((-2 -2, -2 12, 12 12, 12 -2, -2 -2))>
   192→    >>> buffer(square, -2, join_style="mitre")
   193→    <POLYGON ((2 2, 2 8, 8 8, 8 2, 2 2))>
   194→    >>> buffer(square, -5, join_style="mitre")
   195→    <POLYGON EMPTY>
   196→    >>> buffer(line, float("nan")) is None
   197→    True
   198→
   199→    """
   200→    if isinstance(cap_style, str):
   201→        cap_style = BufferCapStyle.get_value(cap_style)
   202→    if isinstance(join_style, str):
   203→        join_style = BufferJoinStyle.get_value(join_style)
   204→    if not np.isscalar(quad_segs):
   205→        raise TypeError("quad_segs only accepts scalar values")
   206→    if not np.isscalar(cap_style):
   207→        raise TypeError("cap_style only accepts scalar values")
   208→    if not np.isscalar(join_style):
   209→        raise TypeError("join_style only accepts scalar values")
   210→    if not np.isscalar(mitre_limit):
   211→        raise TypeError("mitre_limit only accepts scalar values")
   212→    if not np.isscalar(single_sided):
   213→        raise TypeError("single_sided only accepts scalar values")
   214→    return lib.buffer(
   215→        geometry,
   216→        distance,
   217→        np.intc(quad_segs),
   218→        np.intc(cap_style),
   219→        np.intc(join_style),
   220→        mitre_limit,
   221→        np.bool_(single_sided),
   222→        **kwargs,
   223→    )

   228→    geometry, distance, quad_segs=8, join_style="round", mitre_limit=5.0, **kwargs
   229→):
   230→    """Return a (Multi)LineString at a distance from the object.
   231→

   233→    line. For a negative distance it will be at the right side. In general,
   234→    this function tries to preserve the direction of the input.
   235→
   236→    Note: the behaviour regarding orientation of the resulting line depends
   237→    on the GEOS version. With GEOS < 3.11, the line retains the same
   238→    direction for a left offset (positive distance) or has opposite direction
   239→    for a right offset (negative distance), and this behaviour was documented
   240→    as such in previous Shapely versions. Starting with GEOS 3.11, the
   241→    function tries to preserve the orientation of the original line.
   242→
   243→    Parameters
   244→    ----------
   245→    geometry : Geometry or array_like
   246→        Geometry or geometries for which to compute the offset.
   247→    distance : float or array_like
   248→        Specifies the offset distance from the input geometry. Negative
   249→        for right side offset, positive for left side offset.
   250→    quad_segs : int, default 8
   251→        Specifies the number of linear segments in a quarter circle in the
   252→        approximation of circular arcs.
   253→    join_style : {'round', 'bevel', 'mitre'}, default 'round'
   254→        Specifies the shape of outside corners. 'round' results in
   255→        rounded shapes. 'bevel' results in a beveled edge that touches the
   256→        original vertex. 'mitre' results in a single vertex that is beveled
   257→        depending on the ``mitre_limit`` parameter.
   258→    mitre_limit : float, default 5.0
   259→        Crops of 'mitre'-style joins if the point is displaced from the
   260→        buffered vertex by more than this limit.
   261→    **kwargs
   262→        See :ref:`NumPy ufunc docs <ufuncs.kwargs>` for other keyword arguments.
   263→
   264→    Examples
   265→    --------
   266→    >>> from shapely import LineString
   267→    >>> line = LineString([(0, 0), (0, 2)])
   268→    >>> offset_curve(line, 2)
   269→    <LINESTRING (-2 0, -2 2)>
   270→    >>> offset_curve(line, -2)
   271→    <LINESTRING (2 0, 2 2)>
   272→
   273→    """
   274→    if isinstance(join_style, str):
   275→        join_style = BufferJoinStyle.get_value(join_style)
   276→    if not np.isscalar(quad_segs):
   277→        raise TypeError("quad_segs only accepts scalar values")
   278→    if not np.isscalar(join_style):
   279→        raise TypeError("join_style only accepts scalar values")
   280→    if not np.isscalar(mitre_limit):
   281→        raise TypeError("mitre_limit only accepts scalar values")
   282→    return lib.offset_curve(
   283→        geometry,
   284→        distance,
   285→        np.intc(quad_segs),
   286→        np.intc(join_style),
   287→        np.double(mitre_limit),
   288→        **kwargs,
   289→    )

   558→@multithreading_enabled
   559→def make_valid(geometry, method="linework", keep_collapsed=True, **kwargs):
   560→    """Repair invalid geometries.
   561→
   562→    Two ``methods`` are available:
   563→
   564→    * the 'linework' algorithm tries to preserve every edge and vertex in the input. It
   565→      combines all rings into a set of noded lines and then extracts valid polygons from
   566→      that linework. An alternating even-odd strategy is used to assign areas as
   567→      interior or exterior. A disadvantage is that for some relatively simple invalid
   568→      geometries this produces rather complex results.
   569→    * the 'structure' algorithm tries to reason from the structure of the input to find
   570→      the 'correct' repair: exterior rings bound area, interior holes exclude area.
   571→      It first makes all rings valid, then shells are merged and holes are subtracted
   572→      from the shells to generate valid result. It assumes that holes and shells are
   573→      correctly categorized in the input geometry.
   574→
   575→    Example:
   576→
   577→    .. plot:: code/make_valid_methods.py
   578→
   579→    When using ``make_valid`` on a Polygon, the result can be a GeometryCollection. For
   580→    this example this is the case when the 'linework' ``method`` is used. LineStrings in
   581→    the result are drawn in red.
   582→
   583→    Parameters
   584→    ----------
   585→    geometry : Geometry or array_like
   586→        Geometry or geometries to repair.
   587→    method : {'linework', 'structure'}, default 'linework'
   588→        Algorithm to use when repairing geometry. 'structure'
   589→        requires GEOS >= 3.10.
   590→
   591→        .. versionadded:: 2.1.0
   592→    keep_collapsed : bool, default True
   593→        For the 'structure' method, True will keep components that have collapsed into a
   594→        lower dimensionality. For example, a ring collapsing to a line, or a line
   595→        collapsing to a point. Must be True for the 'linework' method.
   596→
   597→        .. versionadded:: 2.1.0
   598→    **kwargs
   599→        See :ref:`NumPy ufunc docs <ufuncs.kwargs>` for other keyword arguments.
   600→
   601→    Examples
   602→    --------
   603→    >>> from shapely import is_valid, Polygon
   604→    >>> polygon = Polygon([(0, 0), (1, 1), (1, 2), (1, 1), (0, 0)])
   605→    >>> is_valid(polygon)
   606→    False
   607→    >>> make_valid(polygon)
   608→    <MULTILINESTRING ((0 0, 1 1), (1 1, 1 2))>
   609→    >>> make_valid(polygon, method="structure", keep_collapsed=True)
   610→    <LINESTRING (0 0, 1 1, 1 2, 1 1, 0 0)>
   611→    >>> make_valid(polygon, method="structure", keep_collapsed=False)
   612→    <POLYGON EMPTY>
   613→
   614→    """
   615→    if not np.isscalar(method):
   616→        raise TypeError("method only accepts scalar values")
   617→    if not np.isscalar(keep_collapsed):
   618→        raise TypeError("keep_collapsed only accepts scalar values")
   619→
   620→    if method == "linework":
   621→        if keep_collapsed is False:
   622→            raise ValueError(
   623→                "The 'linework' method does not support 'keep_collapsed=False'"
   624→            )
   625→
   626→        # The make_valid code can be removed once support for GEOS < 3.10 is dropped.
   627→        # In GEOS >= 3.10, make_valid just calls make_valid_with_params with
   628→        # method="linework" and keep_collapsed=True, so there is no advantage to keep
   629→        # both code paths in shapely on long term.
   630→        return lib.make_valid(geometry, **kwargs)
   631→
   632→    elif method == "structure":
   633→        if lib.geos_version < (3, 10, 0):
   634→            raise ValueError(
   635→                "The 'structure' method is only available in GEOS >= 3.10.0"
   636→            )
   637→
   638→        return lib.make_valid_with_params(
   639→            geometry, np.intc(1), np.bool_(keep_collapsed), **kwargs
   640→        )
   641→
   642→    else:
   643→        raise ValueError(f"Unknown method: {method}")

  1032→@multithreading_enabled
  1033→def snap(geometry, reference, tolerance, **kwargs):
  1034→    """Snap an input geometry to reference geometry's vertices.
  1035→
  1036→    Vertices of the first geometry are snapped to vertices of the second.
  1037→    geometry, returning a new geometry; the input geometries are not modified.
  1038→    The result geometry is the input geometry with the vertices snapped.
  1039→    If no snapping occurs then the input geometry is returned unchanged.
  1040→    The tolerance is used to control where snapping is performed.
  1041→
  1042→    Where possible, this operation tries to avoid creating invalid geometries;
  1043→    however, it does not guarantee that output geometries will be valid. It is
  1044→    the responsibility of the caller to check for and handle invalid geometries.
  1045→
  1046→    Because too much snapping can result in invalid geometries being created,
  1047→    heuristics are used to determine the number and location of snapped
  1048→    vertices that are likely safe to snap. These heuristics may omit
  1049→    some potential snaps that are otherwise within the tolerance.
  1050→
  1051→    Parameters
  1052→    ----------
  1053→    geometry : Geometry or array_like
  1054→        Geometry or geometries to snap.
  1055→    reference : Geometry or array_like
  1056→        Geometry or geometries to snap to.
  1057→    tolerance : float or array_like
  1058→        The maximum distance between the input and reference geometries for
  1059→        snapping to occur. A value of 0 will snap only identical points.
  1060→    **kwargs
  1061→        See :ref:`NumPy ufunc docs <ufuncs.kwargs>` for other keyword arguments.
  1062→
  1063→    Examples
  1064→    --------
  1065→    >>> from shapely import snap, distance, LineString, Point, Polygon, MultiPoint, box
  1066→
  1067→    >>> point = Point(0.5, 2.5)
  1068→    >>> target_point = Point(0, 2)
  1069→    >>> snap(point, target_point, tolerance=1)
  1070→    <POINT (0 2)>
  1071→    >>> snap(point, target_point, tolerance=0.49)
  1072→    <POINT (0.5 2.5)>
  1073→
  1074→    >>> polygon = Polygon([(0, 0), (0, 10), (10, 10), (10, 0), (0, 0)])
  1075→    >>> snap(polygon, Point(8, 10), tolerance=5)
  1076→    <POLYGON ((0 0, 0 10, 8 10, 10 0, 0 0))>
  1077→    >>> snap(polygon, LineString([(8, 10), (8, 0)]), tolerance=5)
  1078→    <POLYGON ((0 0, 0 10, 8 10, 8 0, 0 0))>
  1079→
  1080→    You can snap one line to another, for example to clean imprecise coordinates:
  1081→
  1082→    >>> line1 = LineString([(0.1, 0.1), (0.49, 0.51), (1.01, 0.89)])
  1083→    >>> line2 = LineString([(0, 0), (0.5, 0.5), (1.0, 1.0)])
  1084→    >>> snap(line1, line2, 0.25)
  1085→    <LINESTRING (0 0, 0.5 0.5, 1 1)>
  1086→
  1087→    Snapping also supports Z coordinates:
  1088→
  1089→    >>> point1 = Point(0.1, 0.1, 0.5)
  1090→    >>> multipoint = MultiPoint([(0, 0, 1), (0, 0, 0)])
  1091→    >>> snap(point1, multipoint, 1)
  1092→    <POINT Z (0 0 1)>
  1093→
  1094→    Snapping to an empty geometry has no effect:
  1095→
  1096→    >>> snap(line1, LineString([]), 0.25)
  1097→    <LINESTRING (0.1 0.1, 0.49 0.51, 1.01 0.89)>
  1098→
  1099→    Snapping to a non-geometry (None) will always return None:
  1100→
  1101→    >>> snap(line1, None, 0.25) is None
  1102→    True
  1103→
  1104→    Only one vertex of a polygon is snapped to a target point,
  1105→    even if all vertices are equidistant to it,
